name: Belém, Pará
title: Belém Cruise Port Guide — a Tender Call at Icoaraci, Ver-o-Peso, and a Brand-New World Heritage Site | In the Wake
description: First-person logbook guide to Belém — you anchor off Icoaraci and tender in, 18 km from the centre, which costs two hours of the day. Ver-o-Peso since 1625, the Theatro da Paz inscribed by UNESCO in July 2026, and the Brazil visa most passengers now need.
twitter_description: Belém is a tender call 18 km out, not a downtown berth. Budget two hours for the transfer, and know that Brazil reinstated visas in 2025.
ai_summary: Belém is a tender call anchoring off Icoaraci, about 18-20 km from the centre — the downtown quay is too shallow. Ver-o-Peso dates from 1625, not 1688. The Theatro da Paz became a World Heritage Site on 27 July 2026.
quick_answer: You do not berth downtown. The Port of Belém's city quay carries a little over seven metres and a world-cruise ship draws more, so ships anchor in Guajará Bay off Icoaraci and tender to a river-boat terminal about 18 to 20 kilometres from the historic centre. Volendam herself did exactly that in January 2026. Budget two hours for the round-trip transfer plus tender queues, which leaves roughly four to five usable hours downtown. Spend them on Ver-o-Peso, the fort beside it, and the Theatro da Paz — which became a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 27 July 2026, three days before this page was written. And check your visa: Brazil reinstated them for US, Canadian and Australian citizens in April 2025.
volatile_notice: Checked 30 July 2026 against INMET, IPHAN, UNESCO and Pará state and municipal sources. Two things are actively moving: a new 710 m deep berth at Outeiro was built for COP30 and cruise ships are still not using it — the port authority cites low tide at cruise arrival and departure times — so the tender arrangement may change before 2028. And Ver-o-Peso was physically rebuilt through 2025 and early 2026, so any description written before then is obsolete.

hero.alt: The Ver-o-Peso market hall at Belém with its blue ironwork and corner turrets, seen across the fishing basin with boats moored in front

intro.heading: A tender call eighteen kilometres from the thing you came for
paragraphs: Belém sits about 120 kilometres up the Pará River from the Atlantic, on Guajará Bay. It is the great port city of the Amazon basin — though not, as almost every guide implies, on the Amazon itself. The commercial quay in the middle of town carries a little over seven metres, and that single number decides the shape of your day: a ship drawing eight or more anchors out in the bay off Icoaraci and sends you ashore by launch.

The transfer costs two hours of a port day before you add tender queues at both ends. That is not a complaint — it is the arithmetic, and knowing it in advance is what separates a good day here from a frustrating one. What is left is enough for the market, the fort and the theatre, and those three are the reason to come.

from_the_pier.v: Tender. Ships anchor in Guajará Bay off Icoaraci; passengers come ashore by launch to the Terminal Hidroviário e Turístico de Icoaraci, opened in October 2025.
About 18–20 km. Budget an hour each way with traffic, and add tender queues at both ends.
Roughly four to five usable hours on a typical 07:00–17:00 call. Plan three things, not six.

from_the_pier.k: Ver-o-Peso to the Forte do Presépio
from_the_pier.v: A five-minute walk. These two are the natural pairing.

from_the_pier.k: Old city to the Theatro da Paz
from_the_pier.v: About 15 minutes by taxi to Praça da República.

pier_note: The Icoaraci terminal is a river-boat facility that cruise tenders use — 650 m² built, five floating docks, capacity around 2,000 passengers a day, with ticket windows, accessible toilets and a few shops. It also serves the local route to Ilha de Cotijuba. It was not built to take a 237 m ship alongside and cannot.
map_intro: Belém stands on Guajará Bay, on the Pará River — not on the Amazon proper, which is beyond Marajó Island and out of reach on a port day. This map opens on the walkable centre, because that is where the day is spent and the pins would otherwise sit on top of one another. Zoom out one step for the two points you reach by boat: the tender landing at Icoaraci, 18 km north, and Ilha do Combu across the Guamá to the south.
map_points: Ver-o-Peso — the market, the doca and the iron halls; the reason to come.
Forte do Presépio — the 1616 foundation point, a five-minute walk from the market.
Theatro da Paz — a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 27 July 2026, on Praça da República.
Estação das Docas — the converted warehouses on the waterfront, and the safe lunch.
Icoaraci and Ilha do Combu — the two you reach by boat. Zoom out to see them.
logbook: An honest note before I begin: I have not stood on the Doca do Ver-o-Peso at first light. What follows is read from the record — from INMET's climate normals, from IPHAN's tombamento file, from UNESCO's inscription of three days ago, from Pará state and municipal releases, from the reported detail of Volendam's own call here in January 2026. Soundings taken in another's wake. When I sail here I will come back and log what I actually found.

The first thing to get straight is the one that shapes everything else. You do not tie up in Belém. The commercial quay in the Reduto district carries, in the Portuguese of the port record, pouco mais de sete metros de calado — a little over seven metres — and não permite atracação de grandes navios. Volendam draws about 8.1. There is no argument to be had with that number, and it is not a theory about what might happen: on 12 January 2026 Volendam herself anchored off Icoaraci and tendered nine hundred passengers ashore, on Belém's own founding anniversary. Every 2026 call has followed the same pattern. You come ashore by launch, eighteen to twenty kilometres from the city you booked this call to see.

There is a deep berth now, and it does not change the answer. For COP30 the Terminal Portuário de Outeiro was rebuilt with a pier of roughly 710 metres, expressly to lie two liners alongside as floating hotels. It works. But it is not being used for this, and the reason is mundane: the state ports company's own explanation is that low tide at the hours cruise ships arrive and depart makes the manoeuvre difficult, tornando Icoaraci a opção mais viável. By 2028 that may have shifted. Do not plan on it.

So the arithmetic of the day is fixed before you wake up. Anchor around seven or eight, tender, an hour on the road each way, all aboard around five. Four to five usable hours downtown, and two of your day spent looking out of a bus window at a city you are trying to reach. Knowing that in advance is the whole difference between a good day here and a frustrating one, because the honest response is to plan three things instead of six.

The three are not hard to choose, and the first of them is Ver-o-Peso. Here I want to be careful with a date that almost every guide gets wrong. The market is usually said to date from 1688, though what actually happened in 1688 — on 21 March, by royal provision — was that the King of Portugal granted the Câmara de Belém the revenue of the Ver-o-Peso, so that the drogas do sertão leaving the colony could not be shipped without clearance. The weighing station itself, the Casa de Haver o Peso, was installed at the igarapé do Piri in 1625. The tax grant is sixty-three years younger than the thing it taxed, and collapsing the two loses more than six decades — it loses the point, which is that the market came first and the state came to it.

The name is a corruption of haver o peso — to have the weight — which runs back through Portuguese to the French avoir du poids, avoirdupois, the Hanseatic weighing standard. "See the weight" is folk etymology. It happens to describe the function exactly, which is why it stuck.

What stands there now is largely 1901: the Mercado de Ferro, a twelve-sided hall of 1,197 square metres in prefabricated zinc and iron, shipped in pieces from England and New York and bolted together on the riverbank — four corner turrets and the Belle Époque swagger of a city that at that moment believed rubber would go on forever.

And then a correction of a different kind, because the market you may have read about no longer exists in that condition. The whole complex was physically rebuilt for COP30 — fish market September 2025, main fair November 2025, cast-iron meat market January 2026, nearly three hundred trading boxes renewed. Any description of a dilapidated Ver-o-Peso describes a city that has been superseded.

The second thing is three days old as I write, and I doubt any printed guide on the ship will have it. On 27 July 2026, at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan, UNESCO inscribed the Theatro da Paz on the World Heritage List under criteria (ii) and (iv). Not alone: it is one of two components of a serial property called Amazonia Theatres, paired with the Teatro Amazonas in Manaus — and the squares are inside the inscription, not buffering it. Praça da República in Belém, Largo de São Sebastião in Manaus. That is deliberate. The nomination is about two river cities that built opera houses to prove something, not about two auditoria.

The theatre opened on 15 February 1878, eighteen years before Manaus, which is a fact worth carrying: the famous one came second. And lining the dates up is where I finally understood why the two were inscribed together rather than separately. UNESCO dates the Amazonian golden age from 1879 to 1912 — so Belém built its opera house the year before the money arrived, and Manaus built its in the middle of it, and inside a generation the boom was gone and both cities were left holding a Belle Époque theatre in the middle of a rainforest. A hundred and forty-eight years later the citation praises them for exactly the thing that ruined the men who paid for them: political and urban ambition. Brazil's twenty-sixth World Heritage property, and the first cultural one in the whole North Region.

The third is the correction I would least like a passenger to learn at the rail. Belém is not on the Amazon. It stands on the right bank of the Baía do Guajará, a sub-estuary where the Guamá, Acará and Moju come together on the flank of the Rio Pará — the southern arm of the delta, cut off from the Amazon's main stem by Marajó, an island roughly the size of Switzerland. The water below you is brown, fresh, tidal and Amazonian — but it is not the Amazon. Say at the mouth of the Amazon and you are right; say on it and you are about a hundred kilometres and one enormous island out.

Which sets a limit on the thing people most want. There is no day trip from here to the Amazon proper, none to Marajó, none to a lodge. What there is — and it is more than a consolation — is Ilha do Combu, ten to fifteen minutes by boat across the Guamá, genuinely dense várzea forest with ribeirinho households living off açaí and cacao, less than a kilometre off a city of 1.3 million. I have set out how to reach it below. It is the honest Amazon answer available on a port day.

The weather deserves a line of its own, because every world-cruise call falls in the worst of it: 3,308 millimetres of rain a year across 224 rain days, and a February-to-April call lands squarely in the peak. But the shape matters more than the total. This is not all-day drizzle; it is a bright oppressive morning, then a violent convective downpour in the early afternoon lasting thirty to ninety minutes, then a cooler evening. Belém sets its appointments by it — depois da chuva, after the rain. Do the market and the old city first thing, be indoors by early afternoon, and carry a poncho rather than an umbrella that will invert. The rain is warm, and passengers who accept it have a better day than passengers who fight it.

Two hard practicalities to settle a long way out, and I have given both their own entries below because getting either wrong is expensive. Brazil reinstated visas for United States, Canadian and Australian citizens on 10 April 2025, and the e-Visa explicitly covers arrival by vessel — it has to be in hand before you board in Florida, not sorted out in the bay. And the yellow fever certificate this voyage requires is French Guiana's requirement, not Brazil's. You need the card either way; it is worth knowing which country is asking, so that nobody argues with a gangway officer about the wrong one.

So the verdict the record kept pushing me toward. Belém is a genuinely great port badly served by its own logistics: a four-hundred-year-old Amazon market just rebuilt, an opera house that became a World Heritage Site this week, a colonial core you can walk in twenty minutes — yet it makes you spend two hours on a bus to touch any of it. Go early, take the transfer seriously, accept the rain, and eat the açaí the way they eat it here: thick, unsweetened, near-black, with tapioca granules and fried fish. Not a smoothie bowl. That is a different fruit in a different country.

What I learned putting this together is narrower than I expected, and it is about dates. Three of the four things worth correcting on this page are a date being quoted for the wrong event: 1688 for a market founded in 1625, a UNESCO listing for one theatre when it was two, a visa rule from 2019 that was reversed in 2025. None of them is anybody's dishonesty. They are all just a fact that stopped being true while the guidebooks went on printing. Belém has changed more in the last eighteen months than most cities change in twenty years, and the useful discipline for a port like this is not to know more than the guidebook — it is to check when the guidebook was written.
cruise_port: This is a tender call, and the reason is a number. The Port of Belém's downtown quay in the Reduto district carries a little over seven metres and does not permit large ships to berth; a world-cruise ship draws more than that. Ships anchor in Guajará Bay off Icoaraci and tender ashore to the Terminal Hidroviário e Turístico de Icoaraci. The Icoaraci foreshore itself is silted — the operative local statement is that the liners would run aground if they came to the waterfront.

The terminal is a river-boat facility that cruise tenders use. Opened on 8 October 2025 and run by CPH, the Pará state ports and waterways company — not the federal Companhia Docas do Pará, which runs the Porto de Belém proper. About 650 m² of building on a roughly 1,000 m² footprint, five floating docks, a covered walkway, ticket windows, accessible toilets and a few shops, with capacity around 2,000 passengers a day. It is also the terminal for the river route to Ilha de Cotijuba. Nothing about it was designed to take a 237-metre ship alongside and it cannot.

Outeiro is the thing that might change this by 2028. A new pier of about 710 metres was completed there for COP30 at a cost of over R$233 million, expressly to berth two large ships, and a cable-stayed bridge to Icoaraci opened on 18 October 2025. It is complete and operational — and cruise ships are still not using it, because low tide at typical cruise arrival and departure times makes the manoeuvre difficult. Watch this one; do not plan around it.
getting_around: The transfer is the day's governing fact. Icoaraci to the historic centre is 18–20 km; allow 40–60 minutes each way in normal traffic and longer at peak. On a call from around 07:00 to 17:00 that is two hours of road before you count tender queues at both ends, which leaves roughly four to five usable hours downtown.

Take the ship's shuttle or a pre-booked transfer for that leg. Expect informal taxi and van touts at the terminal. Uber and 99 both operate in Belém and are the recommended way to move around once you are downtown — a tracked route, a fixed price and no cash handling. Street-hailed taxis are legal; insist on the meter. Whether app coverage is reliable at the Icoaraci terminal for the return leg is not something I could verify, so do not stake your all-aboard time on it.

Downtown, everything worth your morning is walkable. Ver-o-Peso, the Forte do Presépio, the Casa das Onze Janelas, the Largo da Sé and Estação das Docas sit within ten to fifteen minutes of each other along the waterfront and through the Cidade Velha. Only the Theatro da Paz needs wheels, and that is about fifteen minutes by taxi to Praça da República.

Language: Portuguese, and the gap is real — English is limited even in tourism-facing businesses, and Spanish gets you part of the way but is not Portuguese. The city met the January 2026 arrivals with trilingual pocket maps and QR codes, which tells you both that Belém is making an effort and that you should carry a translation app.

intro: The transfer eats two hours, so the honest planning advice is to pick two things, maybe three, and do them properly. There are three coherent shapes to a Belém day, and they do not combine.

groups.heading: Shape one — the city, and the strong recommendation
items: Ver-o-Peso, as early as the tender allows. The 1901 iron market, the fish market, the Doca, and above all the ervanárias — the herb and medicinal-plant stalls with their bark, roots, resins, garrafadas and scented banhos de cheiro. That corner is the most distinctive thing in the city and worth the visit even if you buy nothing. 60–90 minutes. The fish and açaí trade is over by mid-morning, so a 09:30 arrival is late for that and fine for the rest.

Forte do Presépio and the Casa das Onze Janelas, five minutes' walk from the market. The 1616 foundation point of the city on the bluff above the açaí fair, with an archaeology museum, and next to it an 18th-century house — sugar-mill owner's, then military hospital, now a contemporary art museum — whose terrace has the best bay view in the old city. 45–60 minutes.

Theatro da Paz, about 15 minutes by taxi to Praça da República. Guided tours depart on the hour Tuesday to Friday 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00, and Saturday and Sunday mornings; 45 minutes, R$10 full and R$5 half, box office only, maximum 40 people per group, and free on Wednesdays. Closed Mondays. On a big-ship day the cap matters — ship excursions will have pre-booked, independent walk-ups may not get in.

Lunch at Estação das Docas. Three converted riverfront warehouses of the old port, opened in 2000 — 32,000 m² along 500 m of frontage, air-conditioned, safe, on the water. This is where you eat tacacá, maniçoba, pato no tucupi and filhote without taking a chance on a street stall, and it conveniently covers the early-afternoon downpour.

groups.heading: Shape two — the river, for anyone who came for the Amazon
items: Ilha do Combu, 10–15 minutes by boat from the Terminal Hidroviário Ruy Barata opposite Praça Princesa Isabel. An environmental protection area of ribeirinho households living from açaí and cacao, with dense várzea forest and igarapés less than a kilometre from the city shoreline. Riverside restaurants serve river fish and açaí and you can swim. The stop people come for is Dona Nena's Casa do Chocolate — bean-to-bar Amazonian chocolate made on the island.
This is the best honest answer to "can I see the rainforest on a port day" — genuine floodplain forest and genuine river life. It also takes half your day, so it does not combine with the city shape.

groups.heading: Shape three — stay in Icoaraci
items: Icoaraci is Belém's ceramics district, and that is not a euphemism for having nothing. The cerâmica marajoara workshops are here, working in a style drawn from pre-Columbian Marajoara pottery, along with a riverside promenade and the boats to Ilha de Cotijuba from the same terminal you landed at.

Modest against the city, but real — and it costs you no bus time at all. For anyone who would rather have four unhurried hours than two hours of road and three rushed ones, this is a defensible choice rather than a consolation prize.

groups.heading: Not feasible on a port day — say it plainly
items: The Amazon River proper, and Marajó Island — roughly three hours by boat each way. Nothing reaches either and back.
The Museu Goeldi on a Monday or Tuesday; its Parque Zoobotânico opens Wednesday to Sunday, 09:00–16:00, R$3. And the Theatro da Paz on a Monday, which is exterior-only.
Ver-o-Peso and the Theatro and the Goeldi and Combu. Pick two. The transfer has already spent the rest.

outro: On booking. This is one of the ports where a ship excursion earns its price, and not for the reason people usually give. It is not access — Ver-o-Peso is free and the theatre is R$10. It is the transfer: 18–20 km of unfamiliar road each way, a hard all-aboard, a language gap, and a theatre capped at 40 people per tour. What you are buying is a guaranteed return to the tender. A private guide booked in advance does the same job and usually better. Going independent is entirely doable if you are comfortable with app-based transport and start early — but book ahead for the Theatro da Paz if it matters to you, because walk-ups on a big-ship day may not get in.

On safety, briefly — the detail is under Know Before You Go. Belém's homicide rate is genuinely high, and it is concentrated in peripheral neighbourhoods rather than the tourist core; what threatens a passenger is petty theft, and Ver-o-Peso is known ground for it. Daylight, a group, nothing visible, and do not wander into the streets behind the market. Under those conditions the market is safe enough and it is absolutely worthwhile. Anyone who tells you to skip Ver-o-Peso has misunderstood this port.

history: Belém was founded on 12 January 1616 at the Forte do Presépio, on the bluff where the fort still stands above the açaí fair — a Portuguese claim staked at the mouth of the Amazon to keep the Dutch, English and French out of the river. The city grew as the shipping point for the drogas do sertão, the forest products of the interior, which is exactly what the weighing station of 1625 existed to tax.

The Casa de Haver o Peso was installed in 1625 at the igarapé do Piri, on the site of today's market, to weigh goods and collect duty. On 21 March 1688 a royal provision granted the Câmara de Belém the revenue of the Ver-o-Peso — a fiscal transfer sixty-three years later, not a founding, and the source of the date most guides print. The igarapé was filled in around 1803 and its mouth became the Doca do Ver-o-Peso. The original Casa was demolished in 1847; the meat market followed in 1867 and the iron fish market in 1901.

The rubber boom made the city you walk through. UNESCO dates the Amazonian golden age from 1879 to 1912, and the civic buildings of the waterfront and the Cidade Velha are its physical residue. The Theatro da Paz opened on 15 February 1878, just ahead of the money; the Teatro Amazonas in Manaus followed in 1896. When rubber seeds reached Southeast Asia and the plantations there undercut the wild trade, the boom collapsed and left both cities with opera houses they could no longer afford — which is, in the end, why UNESCO inscribed them together on 27 July 2026 as the serial property Amazonia Theatres, under criteria (ii) and (iv).

The most recent layer is only months old. Belém hosted COP30 from 10 to 21 November 2025, and roughly R$4.5 billion of committed works — one Pará assessment puts total investment above R$7 billion — rebuilt the market complex, delivered the Icoaraci tender terminal and the Outeiro pier, doubled the airport's capacity, closed the open drainage canals into linear parks and lit the main corridors. Officials described it as advancing the city's infrastructure by twenty to thirty years. Whatever you read about Belém that was written before late 2025 describes a different place.
food: Açaí here is a savoury staple, not a smoothie bowl. It arrives at the Doca do Ver-o-Peso by boat before dawn from the river islands, in baskets called rasas, and it is eaten thick, unsweetened and near-purple-black with farinha de tapioca and fried fish or shrimp. Trying it the way the city eats it is ninety seconds of your day and the most authentic thing available in them. Buy it from an established vendor or a restaurant rather than a street cart — contaminated pulp is a genuine if small transmission route for Chagas disease.

The Pará kitchen is its own thing and it is worth ordering blind. Tacacá — a hot tucupi broth with jambu, the leaf that numbs your mouth, and dried shrimp. Maniçoba, cassava leaf cooked for days. Pato no tucupi, duck in fermented cassava juice. Filhote, pirarucu and tambaqui from the river. None of it tastes like anywhere else in Brazil.

Estação das Docas is the sensible place to eat on a ship day — air-conditioned, safe, on the water, and it covers the afternoon downpour. Cards are widely accepted there and in formal restaurants; carry small-denomination reais for the market, the açaí fair, taxis and the Icoaraci workshops, which are cash-first. Restaurants add a 10% taxa de serviço and nothing further is expected. Always pay in reais, never in the currency your card offers you. Do not drink the tap water; bottled is cheap and everywhere, and ice at established restaurants is fine.
notices: US, Canadian and Australian citizens need a Brazilian e-Visa. The 2019 waiver was reversed on 10 April 2025 and the requirement is in force — about US$80.90, applied for online, 48–72 hours, and it explicitly covers arrival by vessel. It must be in hand before you board. Re-verify before a 2028 sailing: this policy has flipped twice in a decade.

Yellow fever is recommended for Pará but not required to enter Brazil. The mandatory requirement on this itinerary comes from French Guiana, so you will be carrying the certificate anyway. Get the vaccine at least 10 days before, and carry the yellow card.
This is a tender call 18–20 km from the city. Not a walk-off port, not a downtown berth. Budget two hours of road plus tender queues and plan around four to five usable hours in the centre.

Dengue, chikungunya, Zika and Oropouche circulate in Pará, carried by day-biting mosquitoes — precisely when you are ashore. Repellent applied in the morning is the single most useful health measure of the day. Urban malaria risk in Belém itself is low.

Petty theft is the real risk, not violent crime. Ver-o-Peso and the streets behind it are known pickpocket and phone-snatch ground. Daylight, groups, nothing visible, and do not resist a robbery. Brazil is US State Department Level 2 as of 10 June 2026; Pará is not among the states carrying Level 4 advisories.

Plan on rain. A February-to-April call falls in the wettest window of one of the wettest large cities on Earth — March averages 506 mm across 26 rain days. Outdoor walking first thing, indoors by early afternoon, poncho not umbrella.
depth_intro: Things about this call that only make sense once someone says them:
depth_items: Ver-o-Peso dates from 1625, not 1688. The 1688 royal provision granted the city's chamber the market's revenue, sixty-three years after the weighing station was installed. Almost every guide prints the tax date as the founding date.
Belém is not on the Amazon. It is on Guajará Bay, off the Rio Pará — the delta's southern arm, separated from the main stem by Marajó Island. At the mouth of the Amazon, not on it.

The theatre became a World Heritage Site on 27 July 2026, as one of two components of Amazonia Theatres with Manaus — and both public squares are inside the inscription. It is also eighteen years older than the famous one in Manaus.

There is a deep berth and ships do not use it. Outeiro's 710 m pier was finished for COP30 and works; low tide at cruise arrival and departure hours keeps the fleet anchored off Icoaraci instead. The one thing most likely to change by 2028.
The "2,000 stalls" figure is nobody's. The municipality counts 1,193 permit-holders and about 2,400 people working the complex daily.
The market you may have read about was rebuilt. Fish market September 2025, main fair November 2025, meat market January 2026. Pre-2025 descriptions are obsolete, and that goes for most of the city.
practical: Currency: the Brazilian real. Cards are widely accepted in restaurants, Estação das Docas and formal shops; the market, the açaí fair, taxis and the ceramics workshops are cash-first, so carry small notes. Pix is near-universal among Brazilians but needs a Brazilian account and is no use to a visitor. Use ATMs inside bank branches or at Estação das Docas, in daylight, and always decline the card machine's offer to charge you in dollars.
Language: Portuguese, and the gap is real. English is limited even in tourism-facing businesses. A translation app is genuinely useful here rather than a nicety.

Heat and humidity are the constant. Highs of 31–33 °C and humidity of 79–90% every month of the year, with the heat index frequently over 40. There is no cool season and no seasonal relief — what changes through the year is cloud and rain, not temperature. Light long sleeves beat sunscreen alone, and drink more than seems necessary.

Accessibility. This is a tender port, which rules it out for many wheelchair users before anything else is considered, and the terminal at Icoaraci does at least have accessible toilets and a covered walkway. Once downtown the historic core has uneven colonial paving, kerbs and market crowds. Minimal walking: Estação das Docas, which is level, air-conditioned, safe and on the water — a genuinely pleasant place to spend a few hours. Moderate: the market and the waterfront, on the flat. High energy: the Cidade Velha, the fort and the walk up from the açaí fair. Heat and humidity raise the effort of everything by a category.

What it costs: very little once you are there. Ver-o-Peso is free, the Theatro da Paz is R$10 with a 45-minute tour and free on Wednesdays, the Museu Goeldi's park is R$3. The money in this port day goes on the transfer, not on admission — which is exactly what a ship excursion is selling you.

glance.v: Equatorial and flat — mean maxima 31–33 °C and minima 23 °C every month, an annual range of 1.3 °C
79–90% all year; March is the most oppressive month at 89.7%
3,308 mm a year across 224 rain days — rain on 61% of all days. March peaks at 506 mm over 26 days; September is the low at 120 mm
About 2,287 hours a year, bottoming out in February at 105 hours — roughly 3.7 hours a day
Light and variable for most of the day — this is equatorial doldrums air, not a trade-wind coast. The wind that matters arrives inside the afternoon squalls, in short strong bursts across Guajará Bay
One degree south of the equator: close to 12 hours, year-round
Bright oppressive morning, cloud from late morning, a violent 30–90 minute downpour in the early afternoon, a cooler evening

activities.v: Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun

weather.avoid_reason: The wettest quarter of one of the wettest large cities on Earth. March alone averages 506 mm across 26 rain days at 89.7% humidity, and February has the least sunshine of any month. A world-cruise call falls here, so this is advice about expectation rather than about choosing.
catches: There is no dry season, only a less-wet one. September, the driest month, still takes 120 mm across 12 days. Anyone waiting for a dry window in Belém is waiting for something that does not exist.
A world-cruise call lands in the worst of it. February 438 mm, March 506 mm, April 466 mm — 25 or 26 rain days each. Eight hours ashore in March carries roughly an 84% chance of being rained on.

The rain is convective, not continuous — a violent burst in the early-to-mid afternoon lasting 30 to 90 minutes. Belém plans around it. A wet forecast is not a lost day; it is a differently-shaped one.
packing: A light rain jacket or a cheap poncho — an umbrella will invert in a convective squall
Shoes that tolerate being soaked, and a spare pair on the ship

weather.hazard_title: Rain, heat, and a two-hour transfer
weather.hazard_main: Nothing here is dramatic and everything here is cumulative. The rain is near-daily and heavy — 3,308 mm a year over 224 rain days — and a February-to-April call sits in the wettest quarter. The heat never lets up: 31–33 °C at 79–90% humidity every month, with a heat index that frequently exceeds 40 °C. And the 18–20 km transfer from the tender landing means you cannot retreat to the ship when the downpour starts. Convective squalls in Guajará Bay can bring short bursts of strong wind, though the bay is far more sheltered than an open-ocean anchorage.
weather.hazard_season: Year-round heat; rain worst December to May, peaking in March
weather.hazard_note: Do the outdoor walking first thing before the cloud builds, have an indoor fallback booked for the early afternoon — Estação das Docas, the theatre, a museum — and carry the poncho rather than the umbrella. COP30's closed-gallery drainage reportedly improved flow capacity by about 40%, so downtown flash flooding should be less bad than older accounts describe.
weather.sources: INMET (Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia), station BELÉM 82191, Normais Climatológicas 1991–2020. Cross-checked against INMET's own March 2023 balance for Belém, which cites the March normal as 506.3 mm — matching the series exactly.

accepted_warnings.why: The logbook is written from the documentary record and says so in its first line. Sight and a little sound are as far as the sources reach; taste, touch and smell would have to be invented, and inventing them in a document that opens by promising the reader it is read rather than lived is exactly the failure recorded in admin/PORT-PASS-HANDOFF.md on 2026-07-30. If telling the truth fails a check, fail the check.

One pivot, and it is earned rather than inserted: Belem opened the Theatro da Paz in 1878, the year before the rubber boom UNESCO dates from 1879, Manaus opened its in 1896, and inside a generation the boom was gone and both cities were left holding a Belle Epoque theatre in the rainforest. UNESCO inscribed them together in 2026 for the ambition that ruined the men who paid for them. A second pivot would have to be manufactured.

8,553 words against a 6,000 recommendation, and the longest page in the corpus (New Plymouth 7,594; Devil's Island 7,107). Two passes removed everything genuinely duplicated: the logbook lost its standalone Volendam-call, Outeiro, Combu and visa paragraphs and one of its two weather paragraphs, the FAQ lost a question fully covered elsewhere, and the excursions safety block now points at Know Before You Go instead of restating it. What remains is load-bearing. This port carries an unusual number of high-consequence corrections at once — a tender call 18 km out that most guides describe as a downtown berth, a visa requirement reversed in April 2025, a UNESCO inscription three days old, a market rebuilt through 2025-26, and a founding date wrong by 63 years in nearly every published source. Note also that the sidebar (Port Snapshot, Key Facts, Plan Your Visit) renders twice for the mobile layout and is therefore double-counted by the validator, which measures body text; roughly 250 words of the total are that artefact rather than prose.

logbook.alt: The Baía do Guajará at Belém, its brown water stretching to a low green far shore under a wide sky
logbook.caption: The Baía do Guajará. Brown, fresh, tidal and Amazonian — and not the Amazon, which is beyond Marajó Island a hundred kilometres away.

logbook.alt: A potter's hands shaping Marajoara-style ceramics at a workshop in Icoaraci, Belém
logbook.caption: Icoaraci, where the tender lands, is Belém's ceramics district in its own right — Marajoara-style pottery, and a defensible way to spend the day if you would rather not spend two hours of it on a bus.

logbook.alt: The Mercado de Carnes Francisco Bolonha at Belém, a cast-iron market hall with arched openings and decorative ironwork
logbook.caption: The Mercado de Carnes Francisco Bolonha, the 1867 meat market of the Ver-o-Peso complex — reopened in January 2026 after a full rebuild for COP30.

logbook.alt: The Theatro da Paz at Belém, its Corinthian-columned neoclassical portico seen from Praça da República
logbook.caption: The Theatro da Paz, opened 15 February 1878 — eighteen years before the famous one in Manaus. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List on 27 July 2026, with the square it stands in.

cruise_port.alt: The fishing port at Belém with wooden boats moored in rows and the Ver-o-Peso market hall behind, seen from the Forte do Castelo
cruise_port.caption: The fishing port and Ver-o-Peso from the fort. This is the waterfront your ship does not reach — the quay here carries a little over seven metres.

getting_around.alt: The riverside promenade at Estação das Docas in Belém, with the converted warehouses on one side and the water on the other
getting_around.caption: Estação das Docas — the old port warehouses, converted in 2000. Walkable from Ver-o-Peso, and the easiest place downtown to sit out the afternoon rain.

excursions.alt: The Forte do Presépio at Belém, a low white-walled Portuguese fort with cannon on its ramparts above the bay
excursions.caption: The Forte do Presépio, where Belém was founded on 12 January 1616. Five minutes' walk from Ver-o-Peso, and the natural pairing with it.

excursions.alt: The Mangal das Garças park at Belém seen from its observation tower, with lakes, walkways and the butterfly house among trees
excursions.caption: Mangal das Garças, from the tower. A riverside park at the edge of the Cidade Velha, and the shortest route to Amazonian birds on a port day.

history.alt: The Theatro da Paz at Belém seen across Praça da República, its portico and pediment above the trees of the square
history.caption: The theatre and its square. UNESCO's inscription covers both — the nomination is about rubber-boom cities that built opera houses to prove something, not about two auditoria.

food.alt: Salt-cured charque and sausages laid out on a butcher's slab in the Ver-o-Peso market at Belém
food.caption: Charque and sausage on the slab at Ver-o-Peso. The market is cash-first; Estação das Docas takes cards.

depth.alt: The Mercado de Peixe at Ver-o-Peso in Belém, its ironwork and turrets floodlit against a night sky
depth.caption: The fish market at night. It reopened in September 2025 after the COP30 rebuild — which is why descriptions of a dilapidated Ver-o-Peso are describing a city that no longer exists.

gallery.alt: The Estação das Docas warehouses at Belém from the water, three long buildings with the old port cranes in front
gallery.caption: Estação das Docas from the river — three warehouses and a passenger terminal along 500 m of frontage.

gallery.alt: The Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi seen from the street through the ironwork of its park railings
gallery.caption: The Museu Goeldi, founded 1866. Its Parque Zoobotânico opens Wednesday to Sunday — closed on the two days a port call is most likely to fall.

gallery.alt: The marble front of the Basílica de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré at Belém, with its rose window, statue of the Virgin and gold-mosaic inscriptions
gallery.caption: The Basílica de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré, built 1909 on the model of St Paul Outside the Walls. Its Círio procession each October is the largest Marian procession in the world — and falls nowhere near a world-cruise call.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to visit Belém?
faq.a: August to November, comfortably — rainfall drops to 120–150 mm and sunshine climbs past 240 hours. A world-cruise call falls in February, March or April instead, the wettest quarter of the year: 438, 506 and 466 mm, with rain on 25 or 26 days of each month. February has the least sunshine of any month; March is the wettest and most humid. There is no good option in that window, only an informed one.

faq.q: What should I pack for the weather here?
faq.a: A light rain jacket or a cheap poncho rather than an umbrella, which will invert in a convective squall, and shoes you do not mind soaking. Insect repellent with DEET or icaridin applied in the morning — the mosquitoes that carry dengue, chikungunya, Zika and Oropouche here bite by day, which is exactly when you are ashore. A hat, high-factor sunscreen and more water than seems necessary: the mean maximum is 31–33 °C every month of the year at 79–90% humidity, and the heat index frequently passes 40 °C.

faq.q: Will rain concerns affect my day in Belém?
faq.a: Almost certainly, and the useful thing is knowing the shape of it. Belém takes 3,308 mm across 224 rain days a year — rain on 61% of all days — but it is convective, not continuous: a hot bright morning, cloud stacking from late morning, then a violent downpour in the early afternoon lasting 30 to 90 minutes. The city plans around it and so should you. Do Ver-o-Peso and the Cidade Velha first thing and be indoors by early afternoon. The rain is warm; passengers who accept it have a better day than passengers who fight it.

faq.q: Does Belém have a storm season, and can this call be cancelled?
faq.a: No tropical cyclones — one degree south of the equator is far too close for them to form — so no hurricane season in the usual sense. What there is instead is a wet season running roughly December to May and peaking in March, and convective squalls that can bring short bursts of strong wind across Guajará Bay. The bay is far more sheltered than an open-ocean anchorage, so the tender operation is less weather-exposed than at somewhere like the Îles du Salut. The greater constraint here is tidal rather than meteorological: arrival and departure are tide-set, and it is the tide window that keeps ships off Icoaraci rather than alongside at Outeiro.

faq.q: Do cruise ships dock in Belém, or is this a tender port?
faq.a: Tender, and not close to the city. The downtown quay carries a little over seven metres and does not permit large ships to berth; a world-cruise ship draws more. Ships anchor in Guajará Bay off Icoaraci and tender to the Terminal Hidroviário e Turístico de Icoaraci, 18 to 20 kilometres from the historic centre — as Volendam did on 12 January 2026. There is now a deep berth at Outeiro, finished for COP30 with a 710 m pier, but ships are not using it: the state ports company says low tide at typical cruise arrival and departure times makes the manoeuvre difficult. That is the thing most likely to change by 2028.

faq.q: Do I need a visa for Brazil?
faq.a: If you hold a US, Canadian or Australian passport, yes. Brazil reinstated the requirement on 10 April 2025, reversing the 2019 waiver, and it remains in force: an e-Visa applied for entirely online, currently about US$80.90, typically issued in 48 to 72 hours, and it explicitly covers arrival by vessel — so it must be in hand before you board. UK, EU and most other nationalities remain visa-exempt for short stays. Re-verify before a 2028 sailing; this policy has flipped twice in a decade.

faq.q: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination?
faq.a: For Brazil it is recommended for Pará but not required for entry. The mandatory requirement on this itinerary comes from French Guiana a few days earlier, which does demand proof — so you will be carrying the certificate regardless. Brazil follows the WHO single-dose-for-life schedule; take it at least ten days before, and carry the yellow card. Worth getting the reason right, so nobody argues about the wrong country at the gangway.

faq.q: Is Ver-o-Peso safe, and is it worth it?
faq.a: Yes and emphatically yes, in that order. It is a working market in a city with a high homicide rate — reported at 71.4 per 100,000 — but that violence is concentrated in peripheral neighbourhoods and organised-crime disputes, not the tourist core. What actually threatens a passenger is petty theft. Go in daylight and in a group, wear no jewellery or watch, keep the phone away, carry one card and modest cash, and do not wander into the streets behind the market. Under those conditions it is safe enough, and it is a four-hundred-year-old Amazon river market that has just been completely rebuilt. Anyone who tells you to skip it has misunderstood this port.

The market dates from 1625, when the Portuguese installed the Casa de Haver o Peso at the igarapé do Piri to weigh goods and collect duty. The 1688 date you will see almost everywhere refers to a royal provision of 21 March that year granting the city's chamber the revenue of the Ver-o-Peso — a fiscal transfer sixty-three years after the fact, not a founding. The iron market standing there now is 1901; IPHAN listed the whole ensemble on 9 November 1977.

faq.q: Is the Theatro da Paz really a World Heritage Site?
faq.a: Since 27 July 2026, inscribed at the 48th session of the World Heritage Committee in Busan under criteria (ii) and (iv). Not alone: it is one of two components of a serial property called Amazonia Theatres, paired with the Teatro Amazonas in Manaus, and both public squares are inside the inscribed property rather than buffering it. Brazil's 26th World Heritage property and the first cultural one in the North Region. Tours run hourly, last 45 minutes, cost R$10, cap at 40 people, and the theatre is closed on Mondays.

faq.q: Can I see the Amazon rainforest on a port day?
faq.a: Not the Amazon River — Belém is on Guajará Bay off the Rio Pará, and the main stem lies beyond Marajó Island, an island roughly the size of Switzerland. What you can reach is Ilha do Combu, ten to fifteen minutes by boat from the Terminal Hidroviário Ruy Barata: genuine várzea floodplain forest, igarapés, and ribeirinho households living from açaí and cacao, less than a kilometre from the city shoreline. That is the honest answer. What is not available on a port day is Marajó, a lodge, or anything upriver.

faq.q: Is this call suitable if I have limited mobility?
faq.a: Partly, and the tender is the first hurdle — it rules the port out for many wheelchair users before anything else is considered. The Icoaraci terminal has a covered walkway and accessible toilets, and the 18–20 km transfer is a seated ride. Downtown, Estação das Docas is level, air-conditioned, safe and on the water — a genuinely pleasant way to spend a few hours rather than a fallback. The Cidade Velha, the fort and the market have uneven colonial paving, kerbs and crowds, and the heat raises the effort of everything by a category.

map_manifest.source: Every point resolved individually against OpenStreetMap on 30–31 July 2026 — by Nominatim search for the named sites, and by an Overpass named-feature sweep of the Ver-o-Peso complex and the Icoaraci waterfront. None is estimated. The port pin is the tender landing at Icoaraci, 18–20 km north of everything else on the map, which is the single most important thing this map has to show. The anchorage position itself in Guajará Bay is not published in any source I could reach and is deliberately not marked.

port_pin.label: Terminal Hidroviário e Turístico de Icoaraci — the tender landing

bbox_hint.note: Belém stands on the right bank of the Baía do Guajará, on the Rio Pará estuary — the southern arm of the Amazon delta, separated from the main stem by Marajó Island. The tender lands at Icoaraci in the north; the historic centre is 18–20 km south.

pois.name: Complexo do Ver-o-Peso
pois.notes: The weighing station dates from 1625; the twelve-sided iron fish market from 1901, prefabricated in England and New York. IPHAN-listed 9 November 1977. Around it: the 1867 Mercado de Carnes Francisco Bolonha, the Solar da Beira, the Doca, and the Feira do Açaí behind the fort. Rebuilt in stages through 2025 and January 2026. About 1,193 licensed traders.

pois.name: Forte do Presépio (Forte do Castelo)
pois.notes: The 1616 foundation point of Belém, on the bluff above the açaí fair, with an archaeology museum. Five minutes' walk from Ver-o-Peso. The Casa das Onze Janelas — an 18th-century house, now a contemporary art museum with the best bay view in the old city — is immediately alongside, as is the Catedral da Sé.

pois.name: Estação das Docas
pois.notes: Three converted riverfront warehouses of the old port plus a passenger terminal, opened 13 May 2000 — 32,000 m² along 500 m of frontage. Air-conditioned, level and safe; the sensible lunch and the indoor fallback for the afternoon downpour. Not where the ship docks, whatever older guides imply.

pois.name: Theatro da Paz
pois.notes: Opened 15 February 1878, eighteen years before the Teatro Amazonas. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List 27 July 2026 as one of two components of Amazonia Theatres, criteria (ii)(iv) — together with Praça da República, which it stands in and which is inside the inscription. Hourly 45-minute tours, R$10, 40-person cap, closed Mondays.

pois.name: Basílica de Nossa Senhora de Nazaré
pois.notes: Built 1909 on the model of St Paul Outside the Walls in Rome — marble, mosaic, and the shrine of Our Lady of Nazareth. About 3 km from the Cidade Velha, a taxi ride rather than a walk. The Círio de Nazaré procession each October is the largest Marian procession in the world; it falls nowhere near a world-cruise call.

pois.name: Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi
pois.notes: Founded 1866, one of the oldest scientific institutions in the Amazon. The visitable Parque Zoobotânico is a compact urban rainforest with manatees, harpy eagles and jaguars. Open Wednesday to Sunday 09:00–16:00, R$3 — closed Monday and Tuesday, which is a real constraint on a fixed port date.

pois.name: Mangal das Garças
pois.notes: A landscaped riverside park at the edge of the Cidade Velha — butterfly house, aviary, an aquatic-life exhibit and a lighthouse-style tower over the Guamá. Close enough to combine with the fort and the Feliz Lusitânia complex. It was on the official welcome tours given to the January 2026 cruise arrivals.

pois.name: Trapiche do Outeiro
pois.notes: The waterfront of the Outeiro district, immediately north of Icoaraci and linked to it by a cable-stayed bridge opened 18 October 2025. This is where the Terminal Portuário de Outeiro was rebuilt for COP30 with a pier of roughly 710 m at a cost of over R$233 million, expressly to berth two large ships. It is complete and operational — and cruise ships are still not using it, because low tide at typical cruise arrival and departure times makes the manoeuvre difficult. The single thing most likely to change this port by 2028.

pois.name: Ilha de Cotijuba
pois.notes: A river island served by the same Icoaraci terminal the tender lands at — around 27,000 passengers a month on the local route, and home to more than 10,000 islanders. Not a realistic port-day trip on top of the city transfer, but it explains what the terminal was actually built for.

pois.name: Ilha do Combu
pois.notes: An environmental protection area in the Rio Guamá directly opposite the city — 10 to 15 minutes by boat from the Terminal Hidroviário Ruy Barata, and less than a kilometre off the shoreline. Dense várzea forest, igarapés, ribeirinho households living from açaí and cacao, and a bean-to-bar chocolate maker on the island. The best answer to "can I see the rainforest on a port day."

fit.why: Auto-fit spans the 18 km from the Icoaraci tender landing to a historic centre 2 km across, and collapses every downtown marker into one clump — measured at 5-11 px between neighbours in a 678x500 container, against a 36 px marker. The map therefore opens on the walkable centre, where seven of the ten points are. The rule is consistent and stated in the intro: the two boat-distance points, Icoaraci to the north and Ilha do Combu to the south, are one zoom-out away. Nothing is removed from the map.
